html.p: The Timeline dataType renders a horizontal Gantt-style chart where each row is a named entity (machine, process, operator) and each coloured rectangle is a timed event. Activate it with dataType=Timeline.

The visualization handles axis construction, legend creation, colour assignment, and event rendering automatically. You only supply the search data and, optionally, an option string to customise the tooltip, grid layout, or dataZoom.
All Timeline settings support names with a dot. The older names with an underscore still work. If both names are set for a setting, the name with a dot takes priority.
Add visualization_toolbox.hman. before each name in a dashboard option. For example:
The search must return these columns in order:

tr.td: Event start — Unix timestamp in seconds
Event end — Unix timestamp in seconds
Y-axis row label (e.g. machine name)
Legend/colour group (e.g. machine state)
Optional — hex/rgb colour; when the column is missing or empty, colours come from the Splunk palette

html.p: Timestamps must be Unix seconds (not milliseconds). Splunk functions now(), relative_time(), and strptime() all return seconds. The visualization multiplies them by 1000 internally for ECharts.

A palette is a list of colors. Categorical colors give each group a color from that list. In a Timeline chart, the fourth search column defines the group. In this example, that column is state. All Running events share one palette color, even on different machines.
Use timeline.useSplunkCategoricalColors to choose how colors are set. This setting applies to dataType=Timeline, including splitByHour mode.

tr.td: Uses one palette color per category. Ignores any colors in fill_color.
The first four columns are required. Extra columns are allowed.
false (default)
Uses colors from the fifth column. Uses palette colors when values are empty.
Put fill_color in the fifth column. With only four columns, palette colors are used.

html.p: To use palette colors, add this option inside your <viz> element:
You can then return just the four required columns:

Colors follow the order in which categories first appear in the search results. The first category gets the first palette color. The next category gets the next color. Colors repeat after all 60 palette colors have been used.

A category's color can change when the result order or the set of categories changes. The palette does not assign a fixed meaning to a color. For example, Error is not always red. To keep a fixed color, set the option to false and supply fill_color.
Column order matters. With false, the fifth column is read as a color. If it holds extra data, such as hour_index, set the option to true. The hourly example below uses this setting.
Light and dark themes use the same palette colors. The background changes how they look. Compare both previews below. The numbers show the palette order. Each color has its hex code below it.

html.p: The search below simulates a production shift monitor for four machines: CNC-01, CNC-02, Conveyor-01, and Press-01. Each machine transitions between Running, Idle, Maintenance, and Error states throughout the shift. The base time is anchored to 8 hours before the current hour so the chart always shows the most recent shift window.

html.p: Key points about the option string for Timeline:

ul.li: xAxis, yAxis, series, and legend are built automatically — do not define them in the option unless you need to override defaults.
Add dataZoom to enable panning and zooming along the time axis.
Add grid to adjust margins. The left value controls the space for y-axis machine labels — increase it for longer names.

html.p: Set timeline.useSplunkCategoricalColors=false. Add fill_color as the fifth search column. Give each row a valid color, such as #d9534f. Use the same color for every row in a category so the bars match the legend.

pre.code: | eval fill_color=case( state="Running", "#5cb85c", state="Idle", "#f0ad4e", state="Maintenance", "#337ab7", state="Error", "#d9534f", 1=1, "" ) | table start_time end_time machine state fill_color

html.p: Add this option inside your <viz> element:
html.h1: What happens when a color is missing?
html.p: These rules apply when the setting is false or is left out. All rows in a Splunk result table have the same columns. Some rows may have an empty fill_color value. If one row has no color, the whole category gets a palette color.

tr.td: Only the four required columns
One palette color per category.
Every row in a category has a color
Each row uses its supplied color. The legend uses the first row's color.
At least one row in a category has an empty color
All rows in that category use one palette color. Their supplied colors are ignored.

html.p: A mistyped color is not treated as an empty value. For example, #5cb85 is invalid, but it is still passed to the chart. Check your color codes if a bar does not look right.

The chart below uses the default setting, false. Error has a supplied color, so it stays red. Only one of the three Running rows has a supplied color. All three Running rows therefore use one palette color. Maintenance and Idle also use palette colors. Hover over a bar to see its color code.

search.query: | makeresults | eval b=relative_time(now(), "-8h@h") | eval segment=split("CNC-01,Running,0,7200;CNC-01,Maintenance,7200,9000;CNC-01,Running,9000,28800;CNC-02,Running,0,10800;CNC-02,Error,10800,14400;CNC-02,Idle,14400,28800", ";") | mvexpand segment | eval parts=split(segment, ",") | eval machine=mvindex(parts,0), state=mvindex(parts,1), start_time=b+tonumber(mvindex(parts,2)), end_time=b+tonumber(mvindex(parts,3)) | eval fill_color=case(state="Error", "#d9534f", state="Running" AND machine="CNC-02", "#5cb85c") | table start_time end_time machine state fill_color

html.p: Setting timeline.splitByHour=true changes the layout: the y-axis becomes hourly time slots and each machine's events are drawn as bars within those slots. This lets you see — for each hour of the shift — which machines were active, idle, or in maintenance, all on the same chart.

ul.li: The dashboard must be a <form> with a time-range picker using token="time_range" (this page already has one — use the picker at the top).
The search element must bind <earliest>$time_range.earliest$</earliest> and <latest>$time_range.latest$</latest>. The builder reads the time_range token name specifically.
Maximum supported range is 24 hours. Wider ranges produce a warning.

html.p: The chart below works with the existing renderer without any JavaScript changes. It creates a full-hour baseline event for each row, then overlays later state changes inside selected hours. Keep the picker at 24 hours or less; the default range shows the last eight complete hours.

search.query: | makeresults | addinfo | eval range_start=case(isnum(info_min_time) AND info_min_time>0, relative_time(info_min_time, "@h"), 1=1, relative_time(now(), "-8h@h")) | eval range_end=case(isnum(info_max_time) AND info_max_time<=now(), relative_time(info_max_time, "@h"), 1=1, relative_time(now(), "@h")) | eval range_end=if(range_end<=range_start, range_start+3600, range_end) | eval hour_count=ceil((range_end-range_start)/3600) | eval hour_count=if(hour_count>24, 24, hour_count) | eval hour_index=mvrange(0, hour_count) | mvexpand hour_index | eval hour_start=range_start+(hour_index*3600), machine="Packaging-01" | eval segment=mvappend("Running,0,60,0", if(hour_index=2,"Maintenance,20,60,1",""), if(hour_index=4,"Idle,35,60,1",""), if(hour_index=6,"Error,5,53,1",""), if(hour_index=6,"Running,53,60,2","")) | mvexpand segment | where segment!="" | eval parts=split(segment,",") | eval state=mvindex(parts,0), start_min=tonumber(mvindex(parts,1)), end_min=tonumber(mvindex(parts,2)), draw_order=tonumber(mvindex(parts,3)) | eval start_second=start_min*60, end_second=end_min*60 | eval start_time=hour_start+(start_min*60), end_time=hour_start+(end_min*60) | where end_time>start_time | sort 0 hour_index draw_order | table start_time end_time machine state hour_index start_second end_second

  title: {
    text: 'Production Shift - Split by Hour',
    subtext: 'XML-only example: full-hour baseline events with ordered state overlays',
    left: 'center'
  },
  tooltip: {
    trigger: 'item',
    formatter: function (params) {
      var d = params.data;
      var durMin = Math.floor(d.eventDurationInSeconds / 60);
      var durSec = d.eventDurationInSeconds % 60;
      var dur = durMin > 0 ? durMin + ' min ' + durSec + ' s' : durSec + ' s';
      var start = new Date(d.value[10] * 1000).toLocaleTimeString([], { hour: '2-digit', minute: '2-digit' });

  },

        x: ['start_second', 'end_second'],

        var yIndex = api.value(4);

        var end = api.coord([api.value(6), yIndex]);
        return {

          shape: {
            x: start[0],
            y: start[1] - bandHeight / 2,
            width: end[0] - start[0],

          },

html.p: Two options control the visual density of the timeline:

tr.td: Height in pixels of each event rectangle
Vertical gap in pixels between rows

html.p: The older names timeline_bandGap and timeline_bandHeight still work. If both names are set for an option, the name with a dot takes priority.

The chart canvas height is automatically computed as (bandHeight + bandGap) * numberOfRows + gridTop + gridBottom. Set the Splunk panel height option generously (e.g. 600) to ensure the full chart is visible without a scrollbar appearing inside the panel.
Clicking on a timeline rectangle sets the following Splunk tokens that can drive linked searches or dashboard navigation:

tr.td: The internal_name value (machine name)
The category value (state)
Event start (Unix seconds)
Event end (Unix seconds)
Duration in seconds
Fill colour of the clicked rectangle
